name: Topkey API
description:
A JSON:API over the Topkey platform, scoped to a single **account** by a bearer token.

- **Base URL** — `https://api.topkey.io/v1`. Every account-API route is under this `/v1` prefix on the `api.topkey.io` host.
- **Media type** — responses are `application/vnd.api+json`; request bodies are JSON:API documents.
- **Spec** — [JSON:API 1.0](https://jsonapi.org). Resources, relationships, sparse includes, error objects.

## Authentication

Every request carries an account access token as a bearer credential — there is no session and no cookie. The token **is** the account, the user, and the tenant.

```
Authorization: Bearer tk_acct_…
```

Tokens expire after at most **30 days**. Read the calling credential's expiry, last use and permission level with `GET /v1/access_token`. Refresh it before expiry with `POST /v1/access_token/refresh`, which returns a new secret and a fresh expiry; the previous secret keeps working for 5 minutes.

A token inherits its user's current account role; permissions are not frozen onto the key, so changing that membership changes the token's access immediately. Human users may create multiple integration keys without a per-account cap. Agent users are limited to 3 active keys per account.

Send a descriptive `User-Agent` header (for example `AcmeFinance/1.0`) so edge security logs can identify the integration and distinguish it from generic scripted traffic.

A missing, expired, or unrecognized token is a `401`. A valid token whose user is no longer a member of the account is a `403` — membership is re-checked on every request, so removing someone revokes access immediately.

## Authorization

Every endpoint answers two questions: **may this role open this collection?** (a permission — a `403` on failure, whose `detail` names the permission) and **which rows may it see?** (a policy scope — expressed as fewer rows, or a `404` on a show). These are the same Pundit permissions that gate the web app; there is no parallel model to drift.

## Pagination

Collections are **cursor-paginated**, forward-only. There are no page numbers and no total count; order is newest-first.

- `page[size]` — rows per page, default `30`, capped at `100`.
- `page[after]` — the opaque cursor from the previous page's `meta.next_cursor`.
- `meta.has_more` — `true` when another page exists; `meta.next_cursor` carries the cursor.
- `links.next` — a ready-made URL for the next page (present only while `has_more`).

Page by following `links.next` until it's gone. The cursor is opaque — don't parse it. A keyset cursor reads one indexed page at any depth and never runs a `COUNT(*)`, so it stays fast and is stable under inserts.

## Filtering

List endpoints accept `filter[<field>_<predicate>]` parameters, backed by Ransack. Each resource documents and allow-lists a set of index-backed fields. An unknown filter returns `400`, names the valid fields, and points at the parameter in the error's `source`; it is never silently ignored.

```
GET /v1/transactions?filter[approval_status_eq]=pending&filter[flagged_eq]=true
```

## Includes

Use `?include=` to sideload related resources into `included`, avoiding a second round-trip. Relationships whose foreign key is on the row always ship linkage; the rest expose a `related` link you can also just follow. A transaction's `card` and `cardholder` are in the second group: the transaction row holds the provider's card id rather than a card foreign key, so their linkage ships only when you `include` them.

Transaction CSV rows use a display key derived from identifiers already in the API: a coded row is `TK-<transaction year>-<transaction split id>`, while an uncoded row uses the transaction's `external_id`. The split resource's `id` is the stable line identifier; no separate duplicate id is required.

## The response envelope & metadata

Every resource follows the JSON:API envelope: a typed resource with `attributes` and `relationships`, alongside top-level `links` and `meta`.

- **Money is explicit.** Every amount is a `{ "value": "120.50", "currency": "USD" }` object — a decimal string, never a bare float, so nothing rounds through a float.
- **Stable types.** STI and delegated-type models collapse to one stable resource `type`; a consumer never sees an internal subclass name.
- **`meta`** carries pagination signals (`has_more`, `next_cursor`); **`links`** carries `self` and the forward `next`.

## Errors

Errors are JSON:API error objects — an array under `errors`, each with a `status`, `title` and human `detail`. Validation errors point at the offending field with a `source.pointer`.

| Status | Meaning | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `400` | Bad Request | The request asks for something the endpoint can't serve — an unknown `include`, or a filter that doesn't apply; `detail` says what. |
| `401` | Unauthorized | Missing / invalid bearer token. |
| `403` | Forbidden | The token's role lacks the permission; `detail` names it. |
| `404` | Not Found | On another account, or not visible to the role. |
| `422` | Unprocessable | Validation failed, or an operation the record can't perform. |
| `429` | Too Many Requests | Rate limit exceeded. |

## Rate limiting

**100 requests per minute, per token.** The window is keyed by the token, so two tokens on the same account get separate budgets. Over the limit returns `429` with a `Retry-After` header.

## Versioning

The API is versioned in the URL — `/v1` — and follows **semantic versioning**; the first stable release is `v1.0.0`. Only the major version is in the path: minor/patch releases are backward-compatible and ship without a URL change, so `/v1` keeps working across every `1.x` release. **Treat the response as open** — ignore unknown fields rather than failing on them. A breaking change ships as a new major (`/v2`), with `/v1` supported through a deprecation window.

## The approval workflow

Bills, transactions, transfers, expenses and owner payments share one approval pattern, exposed as the same sub-resources under each: `POST …/submissions` (submit), `POST …/approvals` (approve), `POST …/rejections` (reject), and `GET/DELETE …/approval_requests` (history / cancel). Submitting runs the account's real approval workflow, notifications and exemptions included. When no approval rule applies to a transaction (or an exemption matches), submitting moves it to `in_review` with no approval request: there is no pending decision, so `POST …/approvals` returns 403. Approve those through a bulk operation instead (see the guide below).

## Guides

End-to-end recipes for common back-office tasks. Every step is an endpoint documented below; list filters use the `filter[<field>_<predicate>]` syntax, and money compares on `amount.value` (a decimal string).

### Approve the small transactions waiting on you

**1. Ask for exactly the ones you mean.** Both filters are server-side, so the list comes back ready to act on — no client-side sifting.

```
GET /v1/transactions?filter[awaiting_my_approval]=true&filter[amount_lteq]=500
```

- `awaiting_my_approval=true` returns transactions where **your** decision is still pending — not ones you already approved, and not ones waiting on somebody else.
- `amount_lteq=500` ranges over the amount's magnitude, so it means "under $500" whichever direction the money moved.

Both compose with any other transaction filter, and results are newest-first — page with `links.next`.

**2. Approving a handful? Take them one at a time.**

```
POST /v1/transactions/{id}/approvals
{"comment": "Under my approval limit"}
```

The comment is optional. Reject with `POST /v1/transactions/{id}/rejections` instead. Each call returns the updated transaction, so you can watch `approval_status` settle as you go.

**3. Approving a lot? Send one bulk operation.**

```
POST /v1/bulk_operations
{
  "data": {
    "type": "bulk_operation",
    "attributes": {
      "resource_type": "transactions",
      "actions": [{"action_type": "approve", "params": {"approval_comment": "Q3 cleanup"}}]
    },
    "relationships": {
      "items": {"data": [{"type": "transaction", "id": "101"}, {"type": "transaction", "id": "102"}]}
    }
  }
}
```

You get `202 Accepted` with the operation. Poll `GET /v1/bulk_operations/{id}` until `status` reaches `completed`, `partial_success` or `failed`, watching `processed_count` / `success_count` / `failure_count` — and `GET /v1/bulk_operations/{id}/items` for the per-transaction outcome.

`approve` is exclusive: it's the only action allowed in that operation. Use `reject` (with `rejection_comment`) the same way.

Two things worth knowing before you send a large batch:

- **Items you can't act on are skipped, not failed.** Anything you have no pending decision on — already decided, or waiting on somebody else — lands in `skip_count` with a reason on the item, and the rest of the batch still runs. Re-sending the same list is safe.
- **An item that hasn't been submitted yet gets submitted first, then approved.** If you only want to approve things already in flight, build the list with `filter[awaiting_my_approval]=true` (step 1), which by definition only returns transactions that have a pending decision.

`GET /v1/bulk_operations/actions` lists every resource and action available to your token, with each one's parameters.

### Finish your incomplete transactions

A transaction is *incomplete* until it carries everything your account asks for. What that is varies by account — memo, receipt, category, property, work order, and the four accounting dimensions are each switched on or off in your completion rule — so rather than guess, ask.

**1. List them.**

```
GET /v1/transactions?filter[status_eq]=incomplete
```

**2. Ask what a given one still needs.** Either as its own resource, or sideloaded onto the transaction — same object, pick whichever suits your client:

```
GET /v1/transactions/{id}/completion
GET /v1/transactions/{id}?include=completion
```

```json
{
  "data": {
    "type": "transaction_completion",
    "id": "8821",
    "attributes": {
      "status": "incomplete",
      "manually_completed": false,
      "criteria": {
        "memo": "complete",
        "receipt": "missing",
        "category": "missing",
        "property": "complete",
        "work_order": "not_required",
        "accounting_category": "not_required",
        "accounting_location": "not_required",
        "accounting_class": "not_required",
        "accounting_department": "not_required"
      },
      "missing_field_labels": ["Receipts", "Assign Category"]
    }
  }
}
```

Every criterion is always present, so you can render a fixed checklist. Three values:

- `missing` — your account requires it and this transaction lacks it. **This is your to-do list.**
- `complete` — required, and satisfied.
- `not_required` — your account doesn't ask for it. Nothing to do, ever.

`missing_field_labels` is the same wording the Topkey UI shows, if you'd rather display than map.

This is a separate request on purpose: working out the four accounting criteria means running your accounting integration's validations, which is far too slow to attach to every transaction you read. Every transaction carries a `completion` relationship link so you can find it, but the data is only computed when you ask.

For the same reason `include=completion` is **rejected when listing** transactions — on a page of 25 it would be roughly ten seconds of work in one request. It's a per-transaction include. **Ask for it on the ones you intend to fix, not on a whole page.**

**3. Supply what's missing.**

- Code it — `POST /v1/transactions/{id}/splits` with `gl_code_id`, `transaction_classification_id` (the category) and `property_id`, or `PATCH …/splits/{split_id}` to recode the existing split.
- Read receipts — `GET /v1/transactions/{id}/receipts`; every transaction also carries receipt URL and filename metadata in its `receipts` attribute.
- Attach a receipt — `POST /v1/transactions/{id}/receipts` with `url`, or base64 `content` plus `filename` (processed asynchronously, so `receipt` may stay `missing` for a moment after a `202`).
- Read or set the memo — the transaction's `memo` attribute matches the CSV export; `GET`, `POST` and `PATCH /v1/transactions/{id}/memo` address the manual memo resource.

**4. Confirm.** Re-fetch `…/completion` — the criteria you filled read `complete`, and `status` flips to `complete` once none are `missing`.

One thing that can look like a contradiction and isn't: a transaction marked complete by hand reports `status: "complete"` and `manually_completed: true` while individual criteria still say `missing`. That's the override doing its job, not stale data.

### Review the past week's failed bill payments

`GET /v1/bills?filter[payment_status]=failed&filter[created_at_gteq]=2026-08-29` — bills whose most recent payment failed, created on or after the given date (use the ISO date from seven days ago). Results are newest-first; page with `links.next`. `payment_status` accepts `created` / `scheduled` / `processing` / `failed` / `paid` / `canceled`, and composes with any other bill filter.

### Find vendors missing ACH details

`GET /v1/bill_vendors?filter[has_ach_info_eq]=false` — vendors you can't yet pay by ACH, so you can chase their banking details. Banking credentials themselves are never exposed; `has_ach_info` only reports whether they're on file.

## Webhooks

Register an HTTPS endpoint with `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints` (or in Settings > Developer > Webhooks), and Topkey POSTs a signed JSON event to it whenever the account's records change. An account has one endpoint, subscribed to the event types it lists in `enabled_events` (`*` for all). Each event type, with its full payload, is listed under **Webhooks** in this reference.

### The event

```json
{
  "id": "evt_4Zq8mJb1XkTn9RrWc2VhLpYd",
  "object": "event",
  "api_version": "v1",
  "created": 1790000000,
  "type": "bill.status_changed",
  "data": {
    "object": {"id": "5521", "object": "bill", "status": "approved", "invoice_number": "INV-1042", "…": "…"},
    "previous_attributes": {"status": "submitted"}
  },
  "actor": {"type": "user", "id": "88", "name": "Dana Reyes", "email": "dana@example.com", "via": "app"},
  "livemode": true,
  "pending_webhooks": 1
}
```

- `data.object` is the record's attributes as `GET /v1/<resource>/{id}` returns them, flattened beside `id` and `object`, plus `relationships`: `{"id", "type"}` (or `null`) for each to-one relationship whose id is on the record, such as a transaction's `merchant` and `gl_code` or a work order's `property`. To-many relationships, and a transaction's `card` and `cardholder`, are not in the payload; fetch the record for those.
- `data.previous_attributes`, on `.updated` and `._changed` events, holds the old value of each attribute the event changed, and under `relationships` the old linkage of each relationship it changed. The changed attributes in `data.object` are exact for that change; the others are read when the event is sent, a second or two later.
- `actor` is the user who made the change (`via` is `app`, `api` or `mcp`), or `{"type": "system"}` for jobs, integrations, automations and Topkey staff.
- `livemode` is `false` outside production.

### Event types

| Resource | Events |
| --- | --- |
| `bill` | `bill.created`, `bill.updated`, `bill.deleted`, `bill.restored`, `bill.approval_status_changed`, `bill.status_changed` |
| `transaction` | `transaction.created`, `transaction.updated`, `transaction.deleted`, `transaction.restored`, `transaction.completion_status_changed`, `transaction.approval_status_changed`, `transaction.authorization_status_changed`, `transaction.split_added`, `transaction.split_updated`, `transaction.split_removed` |
| `owner_payment` | `owner_payment.created`, `owner_payment.updated`, `owner_payment.deleted`, `owner_payment.restored`, `owner_payment.status_changed`, `owner_payment.approval_status_changed` |
| `property` | `property.created`, `property.updated`, `property.deleted`, `property.restored` |
| `work_order` | `work_order.created`, `work_order.updated`, `work_order.deleted`, `work_order.restored`, `work_order.status_changed` |
| `payment` | `payment.created`, `payment.updated`, `payment.deleted`, `payment.status_changed` |

A status change is its own `<status>_changed` event, and `.updated` covers every other attribute, so a save that approves a bill and edits its invoice number sends both. Archiving or restoring a record is the exception: that save sends only `.deleted` or `.restored`, even if it changed other fields too. Payment activity is a `payment.*` event, never a `bill.*` one, except the bill moving to `paid`, which is a change to its own `status`. `webhook_endpoint.test` is sent by `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints/{id}/test`.

### Delivery

- **Answer 2xx within 15 seconds.** Anything else is a failure, including a redirect, which is never followed. Do the work after you answer.
- **Failures are retried** after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, 5 hours, 10 hours, then every 12 hours, for up to 3 days after the first attempt.
- **At least once, in no particular order.** Dedupe on the event `id`. To act on a record's current state, fetch it rather than trusting the order events arrive in.
- **An endpoint that fails every delivery for 7 days is disabled**, and the people who manage webhooks are emailed. Re-enabling an endpoint disabled this way sends a test event first, and it stays disabled unless that succeeds.
- **History is kept for 30 days**, counted from when the event happened. An event is removed with every delivery of it, including a recent resend, so `GET /v1/webhook_events` and an endpoint's deliveries cover that window, and older events can't be resent.

### Verifying signatures

Every request carries a `Topkey-Signature` header:

```
Topkey-Signature: t=1790000000,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e77a0e56ff536d0ce8e108d8bd
```

`v1` is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of `<t>.<raw body>`, keyed with the endpoint's secret. For 24 hours after a secret rotation there are two `v1` values, one per secret: accept the request if either matches. Compute the HMAC over the raw body as received, since re-serializing parsed JSON changes the bytes, and reject timestamps more than 5 minutes old (or ahead), which stops replays of old requests. Within that window a replayed request looks exactly like a retry, so deduping on the event `id` is what makes handling one twice safe.

In Express, read the body with `express.raw({type: "application/json"})` on the webhook route, not `express.json()`, and pass `req.body` (a Buffer) as the raw body.

Ruby:

```ruby
require "openssl"

# raw_body: the request body exactly as received (request.raw_post in Rails), before any JSON parsing.
def valid_topkey_signature?(raw_body, header, secret, tolerance: 300)
  pairs = header.to_s.split(",").map { |part| part.split("=", 2) }
  timestamp = pairs.find { |key, _| key == "t" }&.last.to_i
  return false if timestamp.zero? || (Time.now.to_i - timestamp).abs > tolerance

  expected = OpenSSL::HMAC.hexdigest("SHA256", secret, "#{timestamp}.#{raw_body}")
  pairs.any? { |key, value| key == "v1" && OpenSSL.secure_compare(value.to_s, expected) }
end
```

Node.js:

```js
const crypto = require("node:crypto");

// rawBody: the request body exactly as received (a string or Buffer), before any JSON parsing.
function verifyTopkeySignature(rawBody, header, secret, toleranceSeconds = 300) {
  const pairs = String(header).split(",").map((part) => {
    const i = part.indexOf("=");
    return [part.slice(0, i), part.slice(i + 1)];
  });
  const timestamp = Number(pairs.find(([key]) => key === "t")?.[1]);
  if (!timestamp || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - timestamp) > toleranceSeconds) return false;

  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${timestamp}.${rawBody}`).digest("hex");
  return pairs.some(([key, value]) => {
    if (key !== "v1") return false;
    // Compare byte lengths: timingSafeEqual throws on buffers of different lengths.
    const given = Buffer.from(value);
    const wanted = Buffer.from(expected);
    return given.length === wanted.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(given, wanted);
  });
}
```

## Security

The serializers are **allow-lists**: a field is exposed only because we decided to expose it. Never serialized — card PAN/CVV/tokens, bank account/routing numbers and beneficiary names, tax ids and dates of birth, cardholder phone, accounting-sync internals, Stripe payment links, or invoice access tokens. You get the non-secret signal instead (`last4`, `has_ach_info`, `is_1099_vendor`, …).

## For LLMs & agents

Machine-readable, low-token versions of these docs, for feeding to an LLM:

- [`/v1/llms.txt`](/v1/llms.txt) — a concise index of the API (the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org) convention).
- [`/v1/llms-full.txt`](/v1/llms-full.txt) — the entire reference as clean Markdown, in one file.
- [`/v1/openapi.json`](/v1/openapi.json) — the raw OpenAPI 3.1 document.

```
    "attributes": {
      "resource_type": "transactions",
      "actions": [{"action_type": "approve", "params": {"approval_comment": "Q3 cleanup"}}]
    },
    "relationships": {
      "items": {"data": [{"type": "transaction", "id": "101"}, {"type": "transaction", "id": "102"}]}
    }
  }
}
```

You get `202 Accepted` with the operation. Poll `GET /v1/bulk_operations/{id}` until `status` reaches `completed`, `partial_success` or `failed`, watching `processed_count` / `success_count` / `failure_count` — and `GET /v1/bulk_operations/{id}/items` for the per-transaction outcome.

`approve` is exclusive: it's the only action allowed in that operation. Use `reject` (with `rejection_comment`) the same way.

Two things worth knowing before you send a large batch:

- **Items you can't act on are skipped, not failed.** Anything you have no pending decision on — already decided, or waiting on somebody else — lands in `skip_count` with a reason on the item, and the rest of the batch still runs. Re-sending the same list is safe.
- **An item that hasn't been submitted yet gets submitted first, then approved.** If you only want to approve things already in flight, build the list with `filter[awaiting_my_approval]=true` (step 1), which by definition only returns transactions that have a pending decision.

`GET /v1/bulk_operations/actions` lists every resource and action available to your token, with each one's parameters.

### Finish your incomplete transactions

A transaction is *incomplete* until it carries everything your account asks for. What that is varies by account — memo, receipt, category, property, work order, and the four accounting dimensions are each switched on or off in your completion rule — so rather than guess, ask.

**1. List them.**

```
GET /v1/transactions?filter[status_eq]=incomplete
```

**2. Ask what a given one still needs.** Either as its own resource, or sideloaded onto the transaction — same object, pick whichever suits your client:

```
GET /v1/transactions/{id}/completion
GET /v1/transactions/{id}?include=completion
```

```json
{
  "data": {
    "type": "transaction_completion",
    "id": "8821",
    "attributes": {
      "status": "incomplete",
      "manually_completed": false,
      "criteria": {
        "memo": "complete",
        "receipt": "missing",
        "category": "missing",
        "property": "complete",
        "work_order": "not_required",
        "accounting_category": "not_required",
        "accounting_location": "not_required",
        "accounting_class": "not_required",
        "accounting_department": "not_required"
      },
      "missing_field_labels": ["Receipts", "Assign Category"]
    }
  }
}
```

Every criterion is always present, so you can render a fixed checklist. Three values:

- `missing` — your account requires it and this transaction lacks it. **This is your to-do list.**
- `complete` — required, and satisfied.
- `not_required` — your account doesn't ask for it. Nothing to do, ever.

`missing_field_labels` is the same wording the Topkey UI shows, if you'd rather display than map.

This is a separate request on purpose: working out the four accounting criteria means running your accounting integration's validations, which is far too slow to attach to every transaction you read. Every transaction carries a `completion` relationship link so you can find it, but the data is only computed when you ask.

For the same reason `include=completion` is **rejected when listing** transactions — on a page of 25 it would be roughly ten seconds of work in one request. It's a per-transaction include. **Ask for it on the ones you intend to fix, not on a whole page.**

**3. Supply what's missing.**

- Code it — `POST /v1/transactions/{id}/splits` with `gl_code_id`, `transaction_classification_id` (the category) and `property_id`, or `PATCH …/splits/{split_id}` to recode the existing split.
- Read receipts — `GET /v1/transactions/{id}/receipts`; every transaction also carries receipt URL and filename metadata in its `receipts` attribute.
- Attach a receipt — `POST /v1/transactions/{id}/receipts` with `url`, or base64 `content` plus `filename` (processed asynchronously, so `receipt` may stay `missing` for a moment after a `202`).
- Read or set the memo — the transaction's `memo` attribute matches the CSV export; `GET`, `POST` and `PATCH /v1/transactions/{id}/memo` address the manual memo resource.

**4. Confirm.** Re-fetch `…/completion` — the criteria you filled read `complete`, and `status` flips to `complete` once none are `missing`.

One thing that can look like a contradiction and isn't: a transaction marked complete by hand reports `status: "complete"` and `manually_completed: true` while individual criteria still say `missing`. That's the override doing its job, not stale data.

### Review the past week's failed bill payments

`GET /v1/bills?filter[payment_status]=failed&filter[created_at_gteq]=2026-08-29` — bills whose most recent payment failed, created on or after the given date (use the ISO date from seven days ago). Results are newest-first; page with `links.next`. `payment_status` accepts `created` / `scheduled` / `processing` / `failed` / `paid` / `canceled`, and composes with any other bill filter.

### Find vendors missing ACH details

`GET /v1/bill_vendors?filter[has_ach_info_eq]=false` — vendors you can't yet pay by ACH, so you can chase their banking details. Banking credentials themselves are never exposed; `has_ach_info` only reports whether they're on file.

## Webhooks

Register an HTTPS endpoint with `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints` (or in Settings > Developer > Webhooks), and Topkey POSTs a signed JSON event to it whenever the account's records change. An account has one endpoint, subscribed to the event types it lists in `enabled_events` (`*` for all). Each event type, with its full payload, is listed under **Webhooks** in this reference.

### The event

```json
{
  "id": "evt_4Zq8mJb1XkTn9RrWc2VhLpYd",
  "object": "event",
  "api_version": "v1",
  "created": 1790000000,
  "type": "bill.status_changed",
  "data": {
    "object": {"id": "5521", "object": "bill", "status": "approved", "invoice_number": "INV-1042", "…": "…"},
    "previous_attributes": {"status": "submitted"}
  },
  "actor": {"type": "user", "id": "88", "name": "Dana Reyes", "email": "dana@example.com", "via": "app"},
  "livemode": true,
  "pending_webhooks": 1
}
```

- `data.object` is the record's attributes as `GET /v1/<resource>/{id}` returns them, flattened beside `id` and `object`, plus `relationships`: `{"id", "type"}` (or `null`) for each to-one relationship whose id is on the record, such as a transaction's `merchant` and `gl_code` or a work order's `property`. To-many relationships, and a transaction's `card` and `cardholder`, are not in the payload; fetch the record for those.
- `data.previous_attributes`, on `.updated` and `._changed` events, holds the old value of each attribute the event changed, and under `relationships` the old linkage of each relationship it changed. The changed attributes in `data.object` are exact for that change; the others are read when the event is sent, a second or two later.
- `actor` is the user who made the change (`via` is `app`, `api` or `mcp`), or `{"type": "system"}` for jobs, integrations, automations and Topkey staff.
- `livemode` is `false` outside production.

### Event types

| Resource | Events |
| --- | --- |
| `bill` | `bill.created`, `bill.updated`, `bill.deleted`, `bill.restored`, `bill.approval_status_changed`, `bill.status_changed` |
| `transaction` | `transaction.created`, `transaction.updated`, `transaction.deleted`, `transaction.restored`, `transaction.completion_status_changed`, `transaction.approval_status_changed`, `transaction.authorization_status_changed`, `transaction.split_added`, `transaction.split_updated`, `transaction.split_removed` |
| `owner_payment` | `owner_payment.created`, `owner_payment.updated`, `owner_payment.deleted`, `owner_payment.restored`, `owner_payment.status_changed`, `owner_payment.approval_status_changed` |
| `property` | `property.created`, `property.updated`, `property.deleted`, `property.restored` |
| `work_order` | `work_order.created`, `work_order.updated`, `work_order.deleted`, `work_order.restored`, `work_order.status_changed` |
| `payment` | `payment.created`, `payment.updated`, `payment.deleted`, `payment.status_changed` |

A status change is its own `<status>_changed` event, and `.updated` covers every other attribute, so a save that approves a bill and edits its invoice number sends both. Archiving or restoring a record is the exception: that save sends only `.deleted` or `.restored`, even if it changed other fields too. Payment activity is a `payment.*` event, never a `bill.*` one, except the bill moving to `paid`, which is a change to its own `status`. `webhook_endpoint.test` is sent by `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints/{id}/test`.

### Delivery

- **Answer 2xx within 15 seconds.** Anything else is a failure, including a redirect, which is never followed. Do the work after you answer.
- **Failures are retried** after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, 5 hours, 10 hours, then every 12 hours, for up to 3 days after the first attempt.
- **At least once, in no particular order.** Dedupe on the event `id`. To act on a record's current state, fetch it rather than trusting the order events arrive in.
- **An endpoint that fails every delivery for 7 days is disabled**, and the people who manage webhooks are emailed. Re-enabling an endpoint disabled this way sends a test event first, and it stays disabled unless that succeeds.
- **History is kept for 30 days**, counted from when the event happened. An event is removed with every delivery of it, including a recent resend, so `GET /v1/webhook_events` and an endpoint's deliveries cover that window, and older events can't be resent.

### Verifying signatures

Every request carries a `Topkey-Signature` header:

```
Topkey-Signature: t=1790000000,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e77a0e56ff536d0ce8e108d8bd
```

`v1` is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of `<t>.<raw body>`, keyed with the endpoint's secret. For 24 hours after a secret rotation there are two `v1` values, one per secret: accept the request if either matches. Compute the HMAC over the raw body as received, since re-serializing parsed JSON changes the bytes, and reject timestamps more than 5 minutes old (or ahead), which stops replays of old requests. Within that window a replayed request looks exactly like a retry, so deduping on the event `id` is what makes handling one twice safe.

In Express, read the body with `express.raw({type: "application/json"})` on the webhook route, not `express.json()`, and pass `req.body` (a Buffer) as the raw body.

Ruby:

```ruby
require "openssl"

# raw_body: the request body exactly as received (request.raw_post in Rails), before any JSON parsing.
def valid_topkey_signature?(raw_body, header, secret, tolerance: 300)
  pairs = header.to_s.split(",").map { |part| part.split("=", 2) }
  timestamp = pairs.find { |key, _| key == "t" }&.last.to_i
  return false if timestamp.zero? || (Time.now.to_i - timestamp).abs > tolerance

  expected = OpenSSL::HMAC.hexdigest("SHA256", secret, "#{timestamp}.#{raw_body}")
  pairs.any? { |key, value| key == "v1" && OpenSSL.secure_compare(value.to_s, expected) }
end
```

Node.js:

```js
const crypto = require("node:crypto");

// rawBody: the request body exactly as received (a string or Buffer), before any JSON parsing.
function verifyTopkeySignature(rawBody, header, secret, toleranceSeconds = 300) {
  const pairs = String(header).split(",").map((part) => {
    const i = part.indexOf("=");
    return [part.slice(0, i), part.slice(i + 1)];
  });
  const timestamp = Number(pairs.find(([key]) => key === "t")?.[1]);
  if (!timestamp || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - timestamp) > toleranceSeconds) return false;

  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${timestamp}.${rawBody}`).digest("hex");
  return pairs.some(([key, value]) => {
    if (key !== "v1") return false;
    // Compare byte lengths: timingSafeEqual throws on buffers of different lengths.
    const given = Buffer.from(value);
    const wanted = Buffer.from(expected);
    return given.length === wanted.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(given, wanted);
  });
}
```

## Security

The serializers are **allow-lists**: a field is exposed only because we decided to expose it. Never serialized — card PAN/CVV/tokens, bank account/routing numbers and beneficiary names, tax ids and dates of birth, cardholder phone, accounting-sync internals, Stripe payment links, or invoice access tokens. You get the non-secret signal instead (`last4`, `has_ach_info`, `is_1099_vendor`, …).
